data.title: Dynex Capital (DX) Could Be 45% Undervalued As Dividend Terms Reset The Debate
data.description:
Dynex Capital (DX) just put fresh income terms on the table. The mortgage REIT approved a quarterly preferred dividend and affirmed its common payout, giving investors updated cash flow figures to weigh against the current share price.

Recent price action has been weak, with Dynex Capital’s share price falling 8.63% over the past month and 13.49% year to date to US$12.18, even though the 1 year total shareholder return of 15.83% and 3 year total shareholder return of 50.36% indicate much stronger longer term momentum.

Bullish investors see Dynex Capital’s pullback and income profile as a mismatch, while cautious holders point to recent price pressure. Which side does the current valuation evidence support next?

Price-to-Earnings of 7.1x: Is it justified?

On basic valuation math, Dynex Capital screens as inexpensive. The stock trades on a P/E of 7.1x at a last close of $12.18, which sits below both the broader US market and the Mortgage REIT peer group that cluster around higher earnings multiples.

P/E compares the current share price with the earnings per share and for mortgage REITs it often reflects how the market weighs income streams against balance sheet and funding risk. A lower ratio can signal that investors are demanding a wider margin of safety for those earnings or that they view current profitability as hard to repeat.

Dynex Capital complicates that simple read. The business shows very large earnings growth over the past year and high net profit margins of 84.7%, and its earnings are forecast to grow around 20% per year, faster than the wider US market. Yet the dividend yield of 16.75% is flagged as not being well covered by free cash flow, debt coverage by operating cash flow is weak, and all liabilities come from higher risk external borrowing. This can justify some caution from income focused investors even when reported earnings look strong.

Compared with the US Mortgage REITs industry average P/E of 8.4x, Dynex Capital trades at a clear discount. Against an estimated fair P/E of 13x, the current 7.1x multiple looks even more conservative. This implies the market is pricing the stock well below a level its earnings profile could potentially support if sentiment or risk perception shifted toward that fair ratio.

data.title: Kardigan (NASDAQ:KARD) Is In A Good Position To Deliver On Growth Plans
data.description:
Even when a business is losing money, it's possible for shareholders to make money if they buy a good business at the right price. For example, biotech and mining exploration companies often lose money for years before finding success with a new treatment or mineral discovery. But the harsh reality is that very many loss making companies burn through all their cash and go bankrupt.

Given this risk, we thought we'd take a look at whether Kardigan (NASDAQ:KARD) shareholders should be worried about its cash burn. In this article, we define cash burn as its annual (negative) free cash flow, which is the amount of money a company spends each year to fund its growth. The first step is to compare its cash burn with its cash reserves, to give us its 'cash runway'.

Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.

How Long Is Kardigan's Cash Runway?

A cash runway is defined as the length of time it would take a company to run out of money if it kept spending at its current rate of cash burn. When Kardigan last reported its June 2026 balance sheet in August 2026, it had zero debt and cash worth US$598m. In the last year, its cash burn was US$215m. That means it had a cash runway of about 2.8 years as of June 2026. Arguably, that's a prudent and sensible length of runway to have. However, if we extrapolate the company's recent cash burn trend, then it would have a longer cash run way. The image below shows how its cash balance has been changing over the last few years.

View our latest analysis for Kardigan

How Is Kardigan's Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

Because Kardigan isn't currently generating revenue, we consider it an early-stage business. Nonetheless, we can still examine its cash burn trajectory as part of our assessment of its cash burn situation. In fact, it ramped its spending strongly over the last year, increasing cash burn by 119%. It's fair to say that sort of rate of increase cannot be maintained for very long, without putting pressure on the balance sheet. Clearly, however, the crucial factor is whether the company will grow its business going forward. So you might want to take a peek at how much the company is expected to grow in the next few years.

How Easily Can Kardigan Raise Cash?

Given its cash burn trajectory, Kardigan shareholders may wish to consider how easily it could raise more cash, despite its solid cash runway. Companies can raise capital through either debt or equity. One of the main advantages held by publicly listed companies is that they can sell shares to investors to raise cash and fund growth. We can compare a company's cash burn to its market capitalisation to get a sense for how many new shares a company would have to issue to fund one year's operations.

Kardigan's cash burn of US$215m is about 14% of its US$1.6b market capitalisation. Given that situation, it's fair to say the company wouldn't have much trouble raising more cash for growth, but shareholders would be somewhat diluted.

So, Should We Worry About Kardigan's Cash Burn?

On this analysis of Kardigan's cash burn, we think its cash runway was reassuring, while its increasing cash burn has us a bit worried. Based on the factors mentioned in this article, we think its cash burn situation warrants some attention from shareholders, but we don't think they should be worried.
